articles.title: In 2021, Lee Marvin’s former 1936 Tucson estate sold for $1.825 million; after a meticulous restoration, the 7,261-square-foot home on 4.19 acres returned to the market with a $5.75 million asking price
articles.summary: In 2021, the former Tucson estate of Oscar-winning actor Lee Marvin sold for $1.825 million, ending decades of ownership by the actor’s family.
articles.body: In 2021, the former Tucson estate of Oscar-winning actor Lee Marvin sold for $1.825 million, ending decades of ownership by the actor’s family. After a meticulous restoration that preserved the home’s historic adobe character while adding contemporary comforts, the 7,261-square-foot property has returned to the market with an asking price of $5.75 million. Mansion Global reports that Marvin’s estate sold the residence to its current owners in 2021, and the new listing reflects both the scale of the renovation and the enduring appeal of architecturally significant desert homes.Located at 5055 North Calle La Vela in Tucson’s Catalina Foothills, the 1936 home was designed by celebrated architect Josias Joesler. It offers seven bedrooms, six and a half bathrooms, a guest house, pool, tennis court, and 4.19 acres of grounds, according to the active listing. The property is now positioned not merely as a luxury residence, but as a rare piece of Tucson’s architectural and Hollywood-linked history.A home with Hollywood historyLee Marvin purchased the estate in 1975 and lived there until his death in 1987. The actor, best known for winning the Academy Award for Best Actor for Cat Ballou in 1966, used the Tucson property as a private retreat away from the pressures of Hollywood. The house remained connected to Marvin’s family for many years after his death. It was finally sold by his estate in 2021 for $1.825 million, nearly 35 years after the actor’s passing, as per reports. That long ownership gives the home an unusually personal provenance, making it more than another high-end desert listing.Marvin was known for his rugged screen presence, but the Tucson estate reveals a quieter side of his life. Set among mature landscaping and open desert views, it offered the privacy and space that appealed to a major film star who valued time away from public attention.The Joesler adobe designThe residence was built in 1936 and designed by Swiss-born architect Josias Joesler, whose work helped define the look of Tucson’s early upscale residential developments. The estate is a classic example of Joesler mud-adobe construction, arranged around an expansive central courtyard with a large fountain.Its original character includes beamed ceilings, four fireplaces, mission-tile porches, chinked mortar, and scored concrete floors. These details give the home a warm, handcrafted quality that contrasts with the sleek finishes found in many newly built luxury properties.The layout connects indoor and outdoor living spaces through arched passageways, a design approach well suited to Tucson’s climate. Rather than treating the desert as something to shut out, the home opens toward patios, courtyards, and mountain views, creating a relaxed Southwestern atmosphere.A careful modern restorationThe current owners undertook a restoration intended to modernise the property without erasing its historic identity. The listing describes the home as fully revitalised, with its architectural integrity preserved and modern systems integrated throughout. The main house now includes a new chef’s kitchen that blends heritage detailing with high-performance appliances. Features include honed marble surfaces, custom cabinetry, a Wolf range, a Sub-Zero refrigerator, custom lighting, and new steel casement windows and doors that open to patios and broad views. This approach appears designed to appeal to today’s luxury buyers, who often want historic charm but expect contemporary kitchens, climate systems, lighting, and indoor-outdoor flow. The restoration therefore adds practical value while retaining the textures and proportions that make the original Joesler design distinctive, as per the reports.Space, grounds, and desert livingThe estate spans 7,261 square feet of living space and sits on 4.19 acres. Its seven bedrooms and six and a half bathrooms provide ample room for family, guests, staff, or a buyer who wants flexible space for work, entertainment, and recreation. Beyond the main residence, the property includes a guest house and a large bonus room with a bathroom. Outdoor amenities include a swimming pool and tennis court, making the estate suitable for both private relaxation and larger gatherings.The grounds are central to the home’s appeal. With mountain and sunset views, expansive outdoor areas, and a courtyard-centred plan, the estate offers the kind of secluded desert lifestyle that is difficult to recreate in a newer development.Why the price has risenThe jump from $1.825 million in 2021 to $5.75 million today is substantial, but the listing reflects more than market appreciation. The home has undergone a comprehensive restoration, and its combination of Joesler provenance, Lee Marvin history, acreage, and luxury amenities places it in a specialised segment of the Tucson market.Historic homes by recognised architects often attract buyers seeking originality, craftsmanship, and a sense of place. When those qualities are paired with celebrity history and extensive modern upgrades, the property becomes especially distinctive.At the same time, the asking price will depend on whether buyers see the restoration and provenance as worth the premium. The estate’s scale, location in Catalina Foothills, and rare surviving Joesler features give it a strong case, but its eventual sale price will show how the market values heritage-led luxury in Tucson.A rare desert legacyLee Marvin’s former Tucson estate is more than a restored celebrity home. It is a 1936 Joesler-designed adobe estate that has survived nearly a century while adapting to modern expectations.For buyers drawn to architecture, privacy, and history, the $5.75 million listing represents an opportunity to own a property with a genuine connection to one of Hollywood’s most memorable actors. For Tucson, it is also a reminder that the city’s older architectural landmarks can remain relevant when restoration respects their original character.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Sandown community hopes Town of Culture will bring change
articles.summary: Sandown was chosen in July as one of 15 finalists from nearly 400 hopefuls across the country.
articles.body:
Sandown on the Isle of Wight is in the final weeks of preparing its bid to become UK Town of Culture 2028.

The seaside resort was chosen in July as one of 15 finalists from nearly 400 hopefuls across the country vying for a £3m prize to stage a showcase of cultural events, with two runners-up each receiving £250,000.

Years of neglect have seen the once thriving tourist hotspot fall into disrepair, with the derelict hotels along the town's seafront becoming a constant target of vandalism .

But locals have told me that winning the Town of Culture competition is the catalyst for change that Sandown needs.

Ed Evans is a glass maker who runs the business his father set up in Sandown 30 years ago.

"Hopefully [winning] will encourage us to do some big public works around the town... that's what we've been asked to do, and I think the town definitely needs some brightening up, there's no doubt about that," he suggests.

"I always talk about the 'Sandown Smile'… on a Summer's day when you go down and everything's happening, it looks as good as any seaside town in the country.

"But then you get a sort of nasty, wet, windy, grey day in the Wintertime and no one's about and there's the tumbleweed blowing and you're looking around at some of the broken down hotels and stuff and you get a feeling that there's a bit of dereliction going on.

"We have potential and there is a lot of good things happening here and if we receive some funding we can show what we're doing here a bit more and just gild the edges.

"A lot of people complain about the town. We want to change that, we want to get rid of the bad spots and highlight the good stuff.

"I love the town, I love the beach particularly. I'm absolutely addicted to going down in the water, and [getting UK Town of Culture] would mean that I feel confident in the future of this place.

"I've never planned to move anywhere or change the premises of the business, and I like to think that we are moving into a better era, so I think it would give us confidence to keep going."

Lyssa Truman has lived in Sandown since she was eight, was made redundant after working for 33 years at the local leisure centre, and now runs exercise classes at The Fitness Hub at the town's old post office.

"I just think there are endless possibilities," she says about the bid.

"There are so many talented people in the area that could do with a break... and I just can see loads of little pop-up cafes, pop-up businesses, little markets where everyone would be able to come together, support each other, but also thrive and grow together as well, and I think that would really attract other people visiting here.

"The derelict buildings and the old hotels, things need to change there, and to just bring that High Street back as well because it was thriving years ago.

"All the different shops were open, and now some are a little run down, and there are lots of empty shops that actually just need to be brought back to life, to give people the opportunity without financially taking hold of them before they even get started.

"There are a lot of beautiful people here and it's not had that injection of money, and I don't think it will take much to make this place absolutely thrive.

"We've got the most beautiful bay in Sandown and when you look at that, you could be anywhere in the world, you really could, but imagine all these little extra things going on too, it'll just be incredible."

Vivette Fryatt, co-owner of the cafe Viv's Cooking, says Sandown remains "special" because of the people.

"I know there's a lot of room for improvement, but guess what? There's a lot also that's going on that's good," she says.

"[With prize money] visitors would see the beauty of Sandown, because in the Summertime they flock and they stay on the beachfront and even people on the island tell them that there's nothing in Sandown and that is so not true.

"Things are happening, things are here already. An injection of cash [could mean] fixing up the seafront, revitalising the High Street, and getting these shops open, even if it's to put community projects in that are attractive to visitors."

Ian Boyd works for environmental organisation The Common Space.

"Sandown sort of almost fizzled into existence in the middle of the 19th century," he explains.

"It evolved overnight as a place for people to come and stay in this beautiful setting and that kind of Victorian idea of tourism has never left, and so the High Street and the seafront were all designed around that model.

"But everything has changed and so Sandown needs to change. A consequence of that is it's struggled and it's had hard times.

"It's perhaps the one place on the island that can genuinely change trajectory... it captures so much of the island spirit, it's a beautiful seafront environment, it's bookended by nationally important landscapes, it's set within a Unesco World Biosphere , it has all of these gifts.

"It has a strong cultural story, it has an amazing diversity of landscapes, seascapes, streetscapes, but it's young enough to change direction, to take a new route, and I think that's what Town of Culture will do for us."

The bid team is putting together a six-month programme of events culminating in the Tide Turner Festival, a major celebration of arts and science.

It would tell Sandown's story over 100 million years from the footprints of the dinosaurs, via Charles Darwin's momentous On the Origin of Species - which he began working on in the town - to the present-day manufacture of pioneering vertipools that provide artificial marine habitats for a changing planet.

The town will find out if it has made it through to the next round of the competition in November.

The overall winner will be announced next year.

articles.title: ‘We had 15-20 versions of the ending’: ‘Drishyam 3’ co-writer Aamil Keeyan Khan reveals they wrote 100 drafts for some scenes, debated Ajay Devgn’s darker side and reworked the climax to surprise audiences

articles.body: ‘Drishyam 3: The Conclusion’ has crossed the Rs 500 crore mark worldwide, adding to the success of the Hindi thriller starring Ajay Devgn, Tabu and Jaideep Ahlawat. In a recent interview, co-writer Aamil Keeyan Khan revealed that the writing team developed 15-20 versions of the ending and rewrote several portions of the screenplay to keep audiences guessing. He also opened up about Akshaye Khanna’s exit shortly before filming, the challenges of introducing Ahlawat’s character and the debate over how dark Vijay Salgaonkar could become.Aamil Keeyan Khan on rewriting ‘Drishyam 3’ with '15-20 versions of the ending’The success of ‘Drishyam 3: The Conclusion’ reflects the risks taken by director Abhishek Pathak and his writing team. Unlike the first two Hindi instalments, which were based on the Malayalam franchise, the third film follows an original story developed for the Hindi adaptation.Speaking to Mid-Day, Aamil Keeyan Khan, who co-wrote the screenplay and penned the dialogues, credited Pathak’s vision and Ajay Devgn’s support for helping the team bring the story to the screen.“Ajay Sir stood behind us like a rock, supporting us in whatever we did. We narrated the first draft to him in April 2025, he loved it. After that, we made a lot of revisions and he was on board with everything,” Khan recalled.The writers faced the challenge of concluding the story of Vijay Salgaonkar and his family, who covered up an accidental murder in the first film. With audiences already familiar with the franchise’s twists and turns, the team had to find a way to deliver a fresh and unpredictable conclusion.Khan revealed that the ending went through numerous iterations as the writers attempted to stay ahead of audience expectations.“We had to set Jaideep sir’s character dynamics with other players, and we had to deliver in seven days! We wrote 100 drafts for some scenes. We even had 15-20 versions of the ending. It was a humongous challenge as people had seen the first two parts and we had to surprise them. A lot of [the script] was scrapped and rewritten in those seven days,” he said.Akshaye Khanna’s exit created a seven-day writing challengeThe film’s development faced another major hurdle when Akshaye Khanna exited the project a week before filming began. The team had to rework the screenplay and establish new character dynamics after Jaideep Ahlawat came on board.According to Khan, introducing Ahlawat’s character required substantial changes to the script, with the writers working against a tight deadline.The team rewrote portions of the story in just seven days, revisiting scenes and exploring different possibilities to ensure the new character fitted into the existing narrative. Khan’s account highlights the scale of the last-minute adjustments required to keep the production moving without compromising the suspense at the heart of the franchise.The extensive rewriting also reflected the challenge of creating an original Hindi storyline while meeting audience expectations for a franchise known for its carefully constructed reveals.‘Is that really Vijay?’: The writers debated how dark Ajay Devgn’s character could becomeBeyond the ending and the changes to the screenplay, one question continued to shape the story: how far would Vijay Salgaonkar go to protect his family?Khan explained that the writers explored several versions in which Vijay became considerably darker before reconsidering whether those choices remained true to the character audiences had followed across the franchise.“Vijay is doing the wrong thing for the right cause. There were so many drafts where he has gone much darker and then we pulled ourselves back, thinking, ‘Is that really Vijay?’ We toyed with the idea of him going completely dark.”The moral conflict at the centre of Vijay’s character has been a defining element of the ‘Drishyam’ films. While his actions are driven by his determination to protect his family, the consequences of those decisions have repeatedly placed him in ethically complicated situations.For the third instalment, the writers had to balance that established characterisation with the need to raise the stakes and deliver an ending audiences would not easily anticipate.‘Drishyam 3: The Conclusion’ box office collectionThe film’s commercial performance has added another milestone to the franchise. By Day 12, ‘Drishyam 3: The Conclusion's total domestic net collection is Rs 323.50 crore and India gross collection is Rs 387.80 crore. Overseas, the film's worldwide overseas gross collection stands at Rs. 501.80 crore.Directed by Abhishek Pathak, ‘Drishyam 3: The Conclusion’ stars Ajay Devgn, Tabu and Jaideep Ahlawat, alongside Shriya Saran, Ishita Dutta and other cast members. articles.title: Vishal Bhardwaj: Gaana Rekha ko hota hai aur gaa main raha hoon
articles.summary: This week, Vishal Bhardwaj was expected to perform at Safdarjung Tomb, but security restrictions in central Delhi necessitated a change of venue.
articles.body: This week, Vishal Bhardwaj was expected to perform at Safdarjung Tomb, but security restrictions in central Delhi necessitated a change of venue. Instead, he performed at a baithak for a small gathering, sharing an evening of conversations and songs. “Last moment pe kisi wajah se hamara venue change hua aur hum yahan pe mil rahe hain. Mujhe lagta hai jo hota hai achhe ke liye hi hota hai ki hum yahan mil rahe hain. Yahan intimacy aur zyada lag rahi hai. Ghazalein aur baatein,” he told the gathering.It was an evening that offered a glimpse of Vishal Bhardwaj the director, screenwriter, lyricist, poet and composer, but foremost, the singer. Seated across from him in the front row, Rekha Bhardwaj listened to his songs from the audience.Mujhe aisa mauka kabhi kabhi milta hai jab main gaa raha hoon aur Rekha sunein: Vishal BhardwajThree years ago, Vishal and Rekha Bhardwaj performed live together for a Delhi audience for the first time. Back then, they spoke of how sharing the stage had been a dream for years. Since then, the two have performed together in Delhi a couple of times. However, this evening at Ibtida-Ek Mehfil belonged to Vishal Bhardwaj, the singer. The stories he narrated drew from his many worlds, while an attentive audience listened, hanging on to his every word.He began the evening with the ghazal “Jaana tumko jaana ho toh mat aana” from Khufiya (2023) and said, “Rekha sang this ghazal. I'm very happy that Rekha is late. She is going to be sitting in the audience today. Mujhe bhi aisa mauka kabhi kabhi milta hai jab main gaa raha hoon aur woh sunein. Usually, ulta hi hota hai. Obviously, hona bhi chahiye. Rekha bahut hi zyada achhi singer hai. Main uske aas-paas bhi nahi hoon. Par ab Rekha nahi hai toh aur bhi mauka banta hai sunane ka.”Sharing a joke, he said, “Gaana Rekha ko hota hai aur gaa main raha hoon.” Later in the evening, when he invited Rekha Bhardwaj on stage, she told the audience that Vishal had been doing more riyaaz than her these days. Vishal added, “Rekha meri guru hai.”Waise maine Meerut se schooling ki, main apne aap ko Dilli se zyada maanta hoon. Mujhe lagta hai main zinda hua ya artiste bana, woh main Dilli ki badaulatMain apne aap ko Dilli ka bashinda maanta hoon: Vishal BhardwajBhardwaj is an alumnus of Hindu College. Whenever he performs in Delhi, he invites his friends to the evening and introduces them to the audience.“Main apne aap ko Dilli se zyada maanta hoon. Waise maine Meerut se schooling ki. Mujhe lagta hai main zinda hua ya artiste bana, woh main Dilli ki badaulat. Main Dilli ke college mein padhne aaya tha Meerut se,” he shared, adding, “Composer toh tha main lekin iss profession mein aane ka mera bilkul bhi iraada nahi tha. Cricketer banna chahta tha, isliye main Delhi University mein aaya tha. Main kharab student tha bahut. Jo admission bhi hua tha, woh sports quota mein hua tha. Isliye Dilli se mera bahut hi alag rishta hai. Main apne aap ko Dilli ka bashinda maanta hoon. Uss daur mein mehfilon ka concept bahut hua karta tha, ki uss waqt ke jo bade-bade artistes hain, woh gaddon mein baith ke gaaya karte thay saath mein. Gaane mein aur sunne waale mein faasla hota gaya. Aur hum log uss cheez ko bhool gaye.”Talking about the concept of a baithak, he said, “Jab audience ko achha lag raha hai toh pata chalta hai, jab achha nahi lagta hai toh pata chal jata hai, toh ye bahut khoobsurat hai.”‘Pata nahi aakhiri baar mohabbat hoti hai ya nahi. Pehli baar toh zaroor hoti hai’Bhardwaj would often stop singing to explain the nuances of the words and the origins of a song. Before singing Pehli baar mohabbat ki hai from Kaminey, he said, “Gulzar sahab ne separation sun ke ye line di thi - pehli baar mohabbat ki hai, aakhri baar mohabbat ki hai. Bahut hi khoobsurat line hai. Waise pata nahi aakhri baar mohabbat hoti hai ya nahi. Pehli baar toh zaroor hoti hai.”He recalled that after recording the song Raat ke dhaai baje, he felt its soul was demanding something else. He then recorded another version of the song.Before performing Paani Paani Re from Maachis, he recalled his lifelong friendship with Lata Mangeshkar, who had asked him to treat her like any new singer, not the legendary artiste she was. He remembered her sincerity, grace and humility.'Pyaar mein itni bhi khamoshi theek nahi, gussa ho toh emoji mein bolo na'Two poets who have left a deep impression on the country, Bashir Badr and Gulzar, kept coming up in Bhardwaj’s anecdotes. Both are immensely close to him, he said and shared, “Bashir Badr sahab mere ustad rahe hain aur woh kehte thay ki ghazal jo hoti hai woh contemporary hoti chali jaati hai aur uska maza bhi tabhi hota hai jab rozmarra ki jo bhasha hai woh usmein use ho. Uska connection tab banta hai. Koshish ye hai ki rozmarra ki baatein ismein ho.”He then sang songs that had references to live location, Gmail and Google Maps. As always, he left the gathering in awe when he sang, “Pyaar mein itni bhi khamoshi theek nahi, gussa ho toh emoji mein bolo na.”'Mujhe toh lag raha tha maine aap logon ko phansa ke rakha hai'Bhardwaj had prepared some new sher by the poet Farhat Ehsas for the audience. He spoke about discovering the poet in Lucknow, and recalled a sher his friend had recited: “Hum log ke umr mein pahunchne ke baad bahut doctors ko consult karte hain. Toh woh tha — ‘Ilaaj apna karate fir rahe ho jaane kis-kis se. Mohabbat karke dekho na, mohabbat kyun nahi karte?’”The audience applauded. Bhardwaj said that he bought the poet’s book afterwards. Towards the end of the evening, he sang two or three ghazals based on his own shers that he had not performed before.“We (all the musicians with me on stage) have been singing all these film songs and looking at each other again and again, thinking that we didn't sing those that we had been preparing,” he said.When he ended the evening on a high note with Chappa Chappa Charkha Chale, requests written on tiny chits began arriving one after another. As the requests kept coming, Bhardwaj said, “Mujhe toh lag raha tha maine aap logon ko phansa ke rakha hai.”This evening reminds me of Gulzar sahab's Dil Dhoondta HaiBhardwaj said the evening reminded him of the old times Gulzar wrote about in the song Dil Dhoondta Hai. He said,“Ghalib ka unhone ek sher leke usko aisa khola ki ‘Dil dhoondta hai phir wohi fursat ke raat din’. Ki woh jo waqt hai na, ki kuch nahi hai karne ke liye, aap apni jaanam ke tasavvur mein bas baithe hue hain. Woh dil dhoondhta hai. Zindagi mein jab hamare ambitions, hamare greed humein itna uljha dete hain, hum wohi lamhein yaad karne ke liye gaane sunte hain. Wohi lamhe yaad karne ke liye hum aisi mehfilon mein saath mein milte hain.”He said,"Ye experience mere liye itna zyada maayne rakhta hai ki main iss mental state mein kabhi-kabhi jaata hoon ki jaise abhi hum log aise baat kar rahe hain, ye itna casual ho gaya hai ki jaise hum log apne drawing room mein baithe hain."Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Farah Khan extends warm greetings to cousin Zoya Akhtar on her birthday
articles.summary: Filmmaker Zoya Akhtar turned a year older on Wednesday.
articles.body: Filmmaker Zoya Akhtar turned a year older on Wednesday. Wishing her on her birthday, her cousin and director Farah Khan shared an adorable picture with her.She first shared a picture with Farhan Akhtar and quipped, "Fru...please wish your sister a Happy Birthday."Farah then posted an image with the birthday girl and wrote a sweet wish."Chal...I will do it myself. Happy birthday Zoya. (Farhan made me do it)," she captioned it.Zoya, daughter of veteran lyricist Javed Akhtar and screenwriter Honey Irani, is known for her projects like 'Luck By Chance', 'Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara', 'Dil Dhadakne Do', 'Gully Boy', among others. She also directed the live-action feature film adaptation of The Archies, which was released on Netflix on 7 December 2023. The film stars Agastya Nanda, Khushi Kapoor, Suhana Khan, Vedang Raina, Mihir Ahuja, AditiSaigal and Yuvraj Menda as Archie Andrews, Betty Cooper, Veronica Lodge, Reggie Mantle, Jughead Jones, Ethel Muggs and Dilton Doiley, respectively.On the other hand, Farah Khan is currently busy with her YouTube channel, which has gained considerable popularity over the past two years, particularly among Gen Z audiences. Her videos featuring food, celebrity home visits and interactions with a diverse range of guests have struck a chord with viewers.She will soon return as a host for the second season of ‘Lock Upp: Sach Ya Sazaa’ alongside Riteish Deshmukh.The announcement comes after the first season received considerable attention from viewers. According to Netflix, the show generated over 5 billion views across social media and word of mouth, with several moments from the series becoming talking points amongaudiences.The first season featured contestants sharing personal stories, facing confrontations and taking part in challenges inside the jail.
